# International Prominence - hill bagging taken to extremes

![Image 3](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375720?fm=jpg&time=1633952687&w=576&h=275&fit=crop&dpr=1&sharp=10&s=ef50a6f029b792c628b61ea2bad1ff54)

© Denise McLellan

Share

 Denise McLellan 

* * *

  
12th October, 2021

This has been read 5,877 times

* * *

Share

**S ome of the UK's more ambitious hill baggers combine British lists with international ascents. They are members of an active worldwide bagging community focussed on mapping, listing and climbing peaks as defined by their prominence relative to adjacent summits, rather than their absolute height above sea level.This network regularly shares data,and occasionally meets to combine resources to achieve trickier summits.**

[![Image 4](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/335234?fm=jpg&time=1594644922&w=152&h=113&dpr=1&fit=crop&s=b20275722be5c52909148198857a712f)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/articles/features/climbing_europes_ultras_with_richard_and_denise_mclellan-12346)

##### Interview Climbing Europe's Ultras with Richard and Denise McLellan

[Read more](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/articles/features/climbing_europes_ultras_with_richard_and_denise_mclellan-12346)

By basing trip objectives around prominence-based lists, mountaineers and hikers can develop a meaningful set of hill-bagging objectives in a relatively small geographical area, going by whatever prominence category they choose.

[![Image 5: Richard McLellan on Norway's Store Lenangstind © Mark Tengove](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375562?fm=jpg&time=1633524618&dpr=1&w=828&sharp=7&s=65b453137eb5219fdbbef0d6a18ab9f9)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=375562)

Richard McLellan on Norway's Store Lenangstind

© Mark Tengove

Given that these hills are relatively prominent, they tend to have great views. Often the interest is not technical, but just identifying a route and communicating with locals can be challenging. Sometimes they are slightly puzzled why you are there at all! Many peak objectives are off the beaten track, with all the joys of route-finding and remote terrain.

International trips need not be expensive or complicated, though they can be. We found that a pre-COVID trip to Spain bagging peaks with a minimum prominence of 1000m was simpler and cheaper than an island bagging trip to Scotland.In contrast, a trip to bag one of the most remote European mountains with a prominence greater than 1500m (Beerenberg, Jan Mayen) was much more complex:

#### European Ultras, taken to extremes - Beerenberg, 2277m, P2277m, Jan Mayen, June 2019

The speck on a map on the middle of the Arctic Ocean which is the ultra-prominence called Beerenberg has had a fascination for me for some time. The Peakbagger website says that geopolitically it's not in Europe, yet being between Svalbard and Iceland, it's an obvious aspiration for anyone who wants to climb European Ultras.

[![Image 6: Traversing the crater rim of Beerenberg © Denise McLellan](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375715?fm=jpg&time=1633950640&dpr=1&w=828&sharp=7&s=672c13ccaf6a295fac45f12fab63f55d)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=375715)

Traversing the crater rim of Beerenberg

© Denise McLellan

After several false starts, a group of 10 of us chartered a 15 berth 50m metal-hulled yacht called 'Valiente' through a Norwegian company called Seil Norge. The plan was to sail four days and 570 miles to Jan Mayen island, land, ascend Beerenberg and a few other peaks, leaving the crew on board, and then sail back, all in two weeks. As is familiar to island baggers, landing was absolutely not a guarantee, and the prospect of seasickness both ways was included in the price.Weather was uncertain with gales, low cloud and poor snow conditions highly possible. And, of course, Beerenberg is a volcano classified as 'dormant' not 'inactive,' with eruptions recorded several times in the last 50 years. The island has no fresh water supply.

The yacht had three professional crew, but we were expected to assist with general duties. The crew and five of the mountaineers were Norwegian, with one Finn, one American (Greg Slayden of Peakbagger website) and four Brits - Richard McLellan, Chris Ottley, Tony Jenkins and me.

We were greeted at Longyearbyen airport, Svalbard, by a huge stuffed polar bear and a warning not to leave the town's boundaries without a gun. Luckily, polar bears, after whom Bear Mountain (or Beerenberg) was named, have long left Jan Mayen island.

[![Image 7: Preparing the Valiente for departure at Longyearbyen © Denise McLellan](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375718?fm=jpg&time=1633950916&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=cc706eec491e1b057707aa6103a10bf1)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=375718)

Preparing the Valiente for departure at Longyearbyen

© Denise McLellan

We soon adapted to life on board, taking turns to cook, make bread, wash down the decks and assist at the helm as we preferred. We learned that those who take seasickness tablets were not seasick, but full marks to Chris and Tony for acting as controls! Actually, the weather was fairly kind to us with light winds and motoring most of the way. The water generator malfunctioned which meant showers were limited but it was generally a comfortable, warm boat with en-suite cabins. We spent much time discussing equipment and approaches to the mountain, trying to plan for all possibilities. There was, of course, no mobile phone coverage, but we got a forecast by satellite phone each day. We saw almost no other ships the whole trip but did get great whale sightings.

Finally, at 01:40 on 11 June 2019, day 4, cloud-topped rocky cliffs came into view. It was our first sight of land since Svalbard. As we had lost any real sense of day and night in the 24-hour daylight, and the weather was relatively calm, the decision was made to attempt landing immediately. The crew felt this was the riskiest bit of the trip and insisted we wore full survival suits as we were ferried ashore on a tiny rubber dinghy with outboard. As the beach (of volcanic grit) shelves very steeply, we had to wade ashore, feeling any moment that the buoyancy of our suits would 'capsize' us. Loads of kit and food for an army was also brought ashore in large waterproof sacks.

After all the planning it was simply magical to have arrived in this dramatic amphitheatre. Walrus Bay was backed by steep grey cliffs disappearing into cloud. Huge, bleached whale bones protruded from the grey volcanic sand and gulls called as they soared above in the swirling greyness.

Jan Mayen island has a permanently staffed Norwegian weather station; the following morning most of the base crew came to visit us as they get few visitors during their six-month posting here. The non-Norwegians had to get formal permission to stay and our passports were duly stamped.The base crew told us the forecast for the next few days was exceptionally good and that we would soon climb above cloud into sunshine. They stressed we had to be self-reliant as they had no means themselves of getting off the island.

[![Image 8: Bivvy on the side of Rudolftoppen © Denise McLellan](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375716?fm=jpg&time=1633950641&dpr=1&w=828&sharp=7&s=951b94fac3b1cfc87cd2bfb6d4cb53d5)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=375716)

Bivvy on the side of Rudolftoppen

© Denise McLellan

So we decided to start out summit attempt that day at 16:30. The landing bay is around 30km from the peak and although there is a gravel track around the coast, the route goes up and down over the mountainous spine of the island. Carrying three days of food, bivvy stuff plus glacier gear meant we had heavy packs.

We were all feeling weary at 22:30 when we suddenly left the valley of fog and entered a mountain of sun and bright snow. The transformation was uplifting! At 23:30, at 650m, roughly at the snowline we bivvyed in bright sun; the views of sharp snowy ridges all around us were amazing.I could hardly believe our luck with the weather.

We set out at 08:30 the next morning, leaving bivvy gear behind, and crossed the snowfield. We roped up where the angle changed and crevasses appeared. It was a straightforward plod in sunshine up the snowy mountain, zigzagging to avoid obvious icy slots and manage the steepness - such a joy to see the whole island above the cloud level.

Finally, at around 16:00, we reached the mighty crater rim, seen from our bivy site, and I realised we really were going to make it. We added crampons for the final icy crest walk to the small, domed and snowy summit and let out a whoop of delight as we reached it, drinking in the cool crisp air and stupendous snowy views.

Then it was time to go down. The cloud briefly lifted off the whole island revealing the coastline - a rare sight indeed. However, the sun made the final snowfield very porridgy. We regained our bivvy site at around 21:00 and had another dried meal and rehydrated, before going to sleep in the brightness, getting burned lips, but drying soaking socks on a rock to a crisp.

[![Image 9: Puffin on Kvalrossen © Denise McLellan](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375717?fm=jpg&time=1633950642&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=25f29338dea959ec5fbc94b5fb665866)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=375717)

Puffin on Kvalrossen

© Denise McLellan

The crew warned that if the forecast changed we might have to leave the island at short notice, but in fact we spent a further four days on land exploring the other even less frequently ascended peaks in small groups, bivvying out above clouds in continuing amazing stable, sunny, dry weather and enjoying a unique feeling of remoteness. In total I walked 95 miles on the island, ascending 14 (some did 16) P100ms (of 18 in total). This number includes two P600ms and the one P1500m ultra prominence.

The lower terrain was most unusual with thick, unstable moss, with some warm and sulphurous gravel patches.Higher up there was snow.We saw lots of birds - puffins, terns, fulmar, great skua, arctic skua and little auks - and some interesting World War 2 defences, amazingly preserved by the cold. It's said to be the only part of Norway not controlled by the Germans during WW2, but the defending troops must have felt very isolated!

The return sail had some final, unexpected excitement. On the second day, in stronger winds and rougher seas, the crew announced that a 'Russian' canvas trawler bag had become caught in the propeller and we could not use the engine. We thus set sail for Bodo, and later Tromso, in northern Norway, many miles further than planned. Luckily, contrary to the forecast, the sea calmed 24 hours later, and the determined crew cut the bag off (2 hours in the cold water).It then transpired that the prop shaft coupling was damaged, and we could only go at low speed. We cooked waffles to boost morale.However, the wind obliged, and the crew also eventually managed to repair the coupling, such that we actually arrived in Longyearbyen only 18 hours later than planned.

Svalbard is a wild 'frontier town' of migrant miners, tourists and reindeer and also a Norwegian tax haven. This makes it just affordable to drink alcohol there. So, it was with mixed feelings that we said goodbye over a beer that night, all delighted that we had achieved our objective with no serious mishap.

The most common prominence-based lists pursued internationally are:

*   Ultras – with over 1500m of prominence
*   Ribus – with over 1000m of prominence
*   Majors - with over 600m of prominence

[![Image 10: Denise on 2900m Tete de L'Estrop in the Provence Alps © Mark Trengove](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/375561?fm=jpg&time=1633524386&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=dfb476e84d6094a26d43058d0b56a86e)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=375561)

Denise on 2900m Tete de L'Estrop in the Provence Alps

© Mark Trengove

In addition, lists of ascents of the World Top 100 by prominence, P2000m, P500m, P300m and P100m are also collated (P = Prominence).

There are a number of useful sources of information:

*   What is prominence? For more information about prominence see a simple explanation on the [UK Relative Hills Society website](https://www.rhsoc.uk/prominence/?utm_content=link1&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig). The Relative Hills Society is a UK-based society which promotes prominence based hill-bagging, particularly in Britain. Its members share information and arrange joint trips.RHSoc also publishes Halls of Fame of number of ascents, in relation to its members and associates only, for Worldwide Ultras, Ribus and Majors each year.
*   For a more detailed examination of the topic see the [Wikipedia Topographic prominence page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_prominence?utm_content=link2&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig)
*   [Peakbagger](https://www.peakbagger.com/?utm_content=link3&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) - Used by many international mountaineers (especially European and American) to log international ascents and trip reports. Run by USA-based Greg Slayden,the website creates 'front runner lists' in which climbers can compare progress against each other.Many of the lists included are prominence-based.There is an excellent associated mobile app for use. It is an invaluable source of information.
*   [Baggers without Borders](https://sites.google.com/site/europeaklist/international-peak-baggers-registers-halls-of-fame?utm_content=link4&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) (BwB) - An international community of baggers who aim to share information to promote international prominence-based lists.Run by UK-based Mark Trengove,BwB publishes annual halls of fame and progress registers, highlighting relative achievements in various international ascent lists (the 2020 Tables can be found here, and subsidiary pages). It also contributes to an international peak-listing project, aiming to improve the quality of prominence-based international lists in less well-mapped/climbed areas.There is also a [Google chat group](https://groups.google.com/g/baggingwithoutborders?pli=1&utm_content=link4&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) through which members share information. To join, contact Mark via the link at the bottom of this page.
*   [Mountain Views](https://mountainviews.ie/summit/340/?utm_content=link5&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) - All you could possibly want to know about hill-bagging in Ireland.
*   [Front Runners list](http://www.cohp.org/writers/AndyMartin/prominence/frl.html?utm_content=link7&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig)- Shows progress on important Prominence lists, both worldwide and by country.The lists are kept regularly updated. Run by USA-based Andy Martin. This is a text/HTML file - you will need to open it after clicking on the link to left. It may be easier to access on a PC than a smartphone.
*   [Top 50 Ultra Prominent Peaks of the World](https://clachliath.com/top-50-ultras-of-the-world/?utm_content=link6&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) - Another fascinating list,regularly updated by UK-based James Stone.
*   [Peaklist](http://www.peaklist.org/?utm_content=link7&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) - This website gives an insight into the work that has gone in to map the world and identify prominence, using what was then rapidly-advancing computing. It has been the source of much of the data on other international mountaineering websites.
*   [Viewfinder](http://viewfinderpanoramas.org/?utm_content=link10&utm_campaign=articles_id_13831&utm_medium=articles_post&utm_source=ukhillwalkig) – a website devoted to relative summit listings, maintained by UK-based Jonathan de Ferranti.

# The P600 Mountains of Britain and Ireland

## Mountains which have a topographic prominence of over 600 metres from any other mountain or land mass

This page includes a map of the mountains of Britain and Ireland which qualify as 'P600 Mountains'. You may use it for reference, or in the completion of your quest to climb all the P600 mountains in Britain and Ireland.   
  
 A P600 is defined as a mountain with a [topographic prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_prominence) above 600 metres, By definition, P600's have a height above 600 metres (1,969 feet), the qualified requirement to be called a "mountain" in the British Isles.   
  
 Essentially, the mountains in the P600 list should all be clearly identifiable, as each has a stand alone mass rising to 600 metres or over.

# The P600 Mountains of Britain and Ireland

## Mountains which have a topographic prominence of over 600 metres from any other mountain or land mass

This page includes a map of the mountains of Britain and Ireland which qualify as 'P600 Mountains'. You may use it for reference, or in the completion of your quest to climb all the P600 mountains in Britain and Ireland.   
  
 A P600 is defined as a mountain with a [topographic prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_prominence) above 600 metres, By definition, P600's have a height above 600 metres (1,969 feet), the qualified requirement to be called a "mountain" in the British Isles.   
  
 Essentially, the mountains in the P600 list should all be clearly identifiable, as each has a stand alone mass rising to 600 metres or over.

 By clicking on any mountain on the map, a pop-out list shows details on the particular mountains height and prominence, in both metres and feet. Grid reference, latitude and longitude are also detailed. Additionally, a link leads you to the Wikipedia page for each individual mountain within the group.

# The Database of British and Irish Hills - past, present and future

Chris Crocker

During 2015, we added the Sibs and made some structural changes around Simms and parents. Internally, Simon Edwardes addressed a growing problem by creating a new database to handle GPS data. Submissions averaged 106 per week, of which 61% were for Tumps below 500m. The increase is very welcome as the database depends on contributors for the majority of its ten-figure grid references. However, checking and validation, discriminating between different summit locations, weeding out dodgy measurements and spotting typographical errors was becoming burdensome. Users have benefited too, as changes from GPS data feed through to hill-bagging much faster than before.

When Graham Jackson and I created the hills database, we never thought it would become what it is today. A number of landmarks have been passed on the journey from 2857 hills and 12 lists to 20657 hills and 40 lists:

2001: version 1 launched

2005: first ten-figure GRs from GPS; data overhaul begins with Wainwright outlying fells

2006: first precision survey - Birks Fell

2008: user survey to guide database development

2009: merger with hills-database.co.uk; Access database revamped

2010: Change control database; Creative Commons licence; second user survey

2011: Irish hills added; editorial team reaches seven

2012: data sharing agreement with MountainViews

2013: completion of data review (7884 hills) using Geograph mapping

2014: Tumps added, doubling database size

2015: hill-bagging.co.uk reaches 5000 registered members; 500 downloads of v14.3.

In the early days we regarded the database as a baggers' tool. The change in our thinking came when we added ten-figure grid references. Many websites gave inaccurate or out of date hill lists. So we decided we would try to offer the best hill data available in a database that we hoped would become definitive. Three-quarters of hillwalking websites and all current Smartphone apps now take data from the DoBIH.

Right from the start the database has benefited from the support of others. The main contributors are acknowledged in the database notes, but many other walkers have reported errors or have improved data on specific hills. In recent years, surveyors have had the biggest impact on data quality. Over 5% of summits in v15.1 have been surveyed to decimal precision. A hundred have come from MountainViews in Ireland, 136 from GJ Surveys, 260 from Myrddyn Phillips and a massive 618 from Alan Dawson. There have also been many col surveys and a further 57 marginal Deweys and Nuttalls have had their drop measured by automatic level and staff.

The DoBIH is demand led. This keeps us customer focused and helps to prevent us from being associated with particular authors or ideologies. It also provides justification for declining requests for new lists, sometimes from authors who see the DoBIH as a means of promoting their baby. We did depart from our policy in version 12 when we added many Scottish P20s. This 'Nuttallisation of Scotland' attracted some criticism. We felt the additions were justified for topographical completeness (and are very useful for identifying future candidates for promotion) but it is unlikely we will do anything similar again. Others think we should focus more on notability. That would be all right if people agreed on what is notable. Meanwhile, we have tempered our policy by anticipating future demand.

Most of the British hills are now in the database and belong to some list or other. It is becoming difficult to invent lists that offer baggers something new and exciting. Some recent proposals are just subsets of the Humps and Tumps. But what about historic lists? The Yeamans have their supporters. We have had requests for Dewey notables, more old English and Welsh 610m lists, and Marsh's lists of Welsh and English hills. All these are long out of print. Are we justified in keeping alive a list that might otherwise fade into oblivion? Should we take a stand against any more subjective lists, such as those derived from guidebooks?

I think the time has come to review the DoBIH's philosophy and policies, with input from our user base. So the next customer survey will go beyond asking about new lists and features. I had intended to run a survey last year. In the event, other things got in the way and we had learned enough from the discussions on the RHB group to know what to do in version 15. There is now a feeling within the team that after all the changes in the last few releases we need a period of consolidation and reflection. Do not expect any major developments for a while.

# Recommended sites for hill walkers and peak baggers

## British Isles focused

[**Relative Hills of Britain RHB**](http://www.rhb.org.uk/) Alan Dawson's website on Marilyns and other relative hill lists of Britain. Includes online versions of the 18 annual Marilyn Hall of Fame Newsletter magazine as well as the ongoing Marilyn Hall of Fame.

[**Hill-bagging.co.uk**](http://www.hill-bagging.co.uk/) Hill Bagging is the online version of the Database of British and Irish Hills. The website is updated on a regular basis. Each hill has its own entry with a range of useful information. If you register on the website you can log your own progress with the lists.

[**Haroldstreet**](http://www.haroldstreet.org.uk/) Mountain Lists, GPS waypoints and hill-walking routes. An alternative website that also hosts the Database of British and Irish Hills data and also many other hill and non- hill lists. The website is updated on a regular basis. If you register on the website you can log your own progress with the lists.

**[TrigpointingUK](http://www.trigpointing.uk/)**Trigpoint Logging System. Obviously, not a relative hill based list. However, there are useful trip reports and there is a very good phone app that allows you to log your tripoint pillars whilst on the hill and by checking the FB number you can confirm you are on the right hilltop.

[**Change Register - The Marilyns of England**](http://mappingmountains.blogspot.com/2020/03/change-register-marilyns-of-england.html)**and [Change Register - The Marilyns of Wales](http://mappingmountains.blogspot.com/2020/03/change-register-marilyns-of-wales.html)**Change Registers to the Marilyns of England and also the Marilyns of Wales, post-TACit Tables publication, are now available on [Mapping Mountains](http://mappingmountains.blogspot.com/). Each includes changes to the Submarilyns.

**[UK Hillwalking](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/)**- UKH is a popular online magazine covering hill walking related news and articles in the UK

[**Ordnance Survey**](http://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/) Ordnance Survey, Britain's mapping agency.

[**Mountain Bothy Association**](http://www.mountainbothies.org.uk/) manages some 100 shelters in some of the remoter parts of Britain with the permission and support of the owners. The shelters are unlocked and are available for anyone to use, even relative hill-baggers.

**[Grough magazine](http://www.grough.co.uk/magazine)**Grough Digital outdoor magazine with a Facebook presence and an emphasis on mountain rescue.

[**Mountain Weather Information Service**](http://www.mwis.org.uk/) Mountain Weather Information Service provide detailed three-day forecasts for the main hillwalking areas of Britain. There is also a phone app.

[**British Geological Survey**](http://mapapps.bgs.ac.uk/geologyofbritain/home.html?) British Geological Survey Geology of Britain viewer. There are two very good phone apps to help you to identify what kind of rock that you just stubbed your toe on.

**[Magicseaweed](http://www.magicseaweed.com/)**The Magicseaweed site is for surfers. However it is useful to know the sea conditions when bagging islands, which are hills surrounded by water, that is often choppy and swelly.

## International focus

**[Peakbagger](http://www.peakbagger.com/)**USA based website with astonishing number of world-wide hill and mountain lists that would take several lifetimes to exhaust the possibilities. Excellent source for the Ultra and Major lists. Equally excellent phone app for Android and iPhones that allows you to store information from the Peakbagger and Summitpost websites for offline use. You can log your bags on the go. Highly recommended.

**[Summitpost](http://www.summitpost.org/)**An invaluable source of information about mountains and mountain ranges throughout the world. Includes lots of trip reports and GPS tracks. Information can be stored on your phone using the Peakbagger app.

**[Europeaklist](http://sites.google.com/site/europeaklist/)**European hill and mountain lists, country by country. A labour of love by Mark Trengove.

[**MountainViews**](http://mountainviews.ie/summit) an outstanding website that covers Ireland. A contender for one of the best hill/mountain websites in the world.

[**Wikiloc**](http://www.wikiloc.com/wikiloc/home.do) has trails of the world. Excellent collection of other people's GPS tracks for when trying to find the path without a British OS quality map.

[**Austrian Alpine Club (UK Section)**](http://www.aacuk.org.uk/) membership includes at no extra charge, Mountain Rescue Insurance; worldwide to 6000m, without age limit and inclusive of repatriation; Alpine Hut Rights; discounted accommodation costs in alpine huts belonging to the National Alpine Mountaineering Federations.

[**Baggers without Borders**](https://www.baggerswithoutborders.org/) - International Peakbaggers' Progress Registers and Halls of Fame. Also contains hill / mountain lists for European countries.

# Recommended sites for hill walkers and peak baggers

## British Isles focused

[**Relative Hills of Britain RHB**](http://www.rhb.org.uk/) Alan Dawson's website on Marilyns and other relative hill lists of Britain. Includes online versions of the 18 annual Marilyn Hall of Fame Newsletter magazine as well as the ongoing Marilyn Hall of Fame.

[**Hill-bagging.co.uk**](http://www.hill-bagging.co.uk/) Hill Bagging is the online version of the Database of British and Irish Hills. The website is updated on a regular basis. Each hill has its own entry with a range of useful information. If you register on the website you can log your own progress with the lists.

[**Haroldstreet**](http://www.haroldstreet.org.uk/) Mountain Lists, GPS waypoints and hill-walking routes. An alternative website that also hosts the Database of British and Irish Hills data and also many other hill and non- hill lists. The website is updated on a regular basis. If you register on the website you can log your own progress with the lists.

**[TrigpointingUK](http://www.trigpointing.uk/)**Trigpoint Logging System. Obviously, not a relative hill based list. However, there are useful trip reports and there is a very good phone app that allows you to log your tripoint pillars whilst on the hill and by checking the FB number you can confirm you are on the right hilltop.

[**Change Register - The Marilyns of England**](http://mappingmountains.blogspot.com/2020/03/change-register-marilyns-of-england.html)**and [Change Register - The Marilyns of Wales](http://mappingmountains.blogspot.com/2020/03/change-register-marilyns-of-wales.html)**Change Registers to the Marilyns of England and also the Marilyns of Wales, post-TACit Tables publication, are now available on [Mapping Mountains](http://mappingmountains.blogspot.com/). Each includes changes to the Submarilyns.

**[UK Hillwalking](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/)**- UKH is a popular online magazine covering hill walking related news and articles in the UK

[**Ordnance Survey**](http://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/) Ordnance Survey, Britain's mapping agency.

[**Mountain Bothy Association**](http://www.mountainbothies.org.uk/) manages some 100 shelters in some of the remoter parts of Britain with the permission and support of the owners. The shelters are unlocked and are available for anyone to use, even relative hill-baggers.

**[Grough magazine](http://www.grough.co.uk/magazine)**Grough Digital outdoor magazine with a Facebook presence and an emphasis on mountain rescue.

[**Mountain Weather Information Service**](http://www.mwis.org.uk/) Mountain Weather Information Service provide detailed three-day forecasts for the main hillwalking areas of Britain. There is also a phone app.

[**British Geological Survey**](http://mapapps.bgs.ac.uk/geologyofbritain/home.html?) British Geological Survey Geology of Britain viewer. There are two very good phone apps to help you to identify what kind of rock that you just stubbed your toe on.

**[Magicseaweed](http://www.magicseaweed.com/)**The Magicseaweed site is for surfers. However it is useful to know the sea conditions when bagging islands, which are hills surrounded by water, that is often choppy and swelly.

## International focus

**[Peakbagger](http://www.peakbagger.com/)**USA based website with astonishing number of world-wide hill and mountain lists that would take several lifetimes to exhaust the possibilities. Excellent source for the Ultra and Major lists. Equally excellent phone app for Android and iPhones that allows you to store information from the Peakbagger and Summitpost websites for offline use. You can log your bags on the go. Highly recommended.

**[Summitpost](http://www.summitpost.org/)**An invaluable source of information about mountains and mountain ranges throughout the world. Includes lots of trip reports and GPS tracks. Information can be stored on your phone using the Peakbagger app.

**[Europeaklist](http://sites.google.com/site/europeaklist/)**European hill and mountain lists, country by country. A labour of love by Mark Trengove.

[**MountainViews**](http://mountainviews.ie/summit) an outstanding website that covers Ireland. A contender for one of the best hill/mountain websites in the world.

[**Wikiloc**](http://www.wikiloc.com/wikiloc/home.do) has trails of the world. Excellent collection of other people's GPS tracks for when trying to find the path without a British OS quality map.

[**Austrian Alpine Club (UK Section)**](http://www.aacuk.org.uk/) membership includes at no extra charge, Mountain Rescue Insurance; worldwide to 6000m, without age limit and inclusive of repatriation; Alpine Hut Rights; discounted accommodation costs in alpine huts belonging to the National Alpine Mountaineering Federations.

[**Baggers without Borders**](https://www.baggerswithoutborders.org/) - International Peakbaggers' Progress Registers and Halls of Fame. Also contains hill / mountain lists for European countries.

# The P600 Challenge - Fastest round of the 600m-prominence peaks

![Image 3](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462576?fm=jpg&time=1757078448&w=576&h=275&dpr=1&sharp=10&crop=1079%2C515%2C0%2C386&s=2694448090f83853f1ff2edbfc12135b)

© Simon Tull

Share

[![Image 4](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462592?fm=jpg&time=1757089747&w=195&h=130&fit=crop&s=f5aaea5f5567b8a2f2377724df0c73d9)![Image 5](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462592?fm=jpg&time=1757089747&w=90&h=60&fit=crop&dpr=1&s=f05cc9c33e542d644c72d139ee03f1ee)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/user/profile.php?id=430538)[Simon Tull](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/user/profile.php?id=430538)

* * *

  
6th October, 2025

This has been read 4,214 times

* * *

Share

_Each rises 600m or more from its surroundings; there are 119 of them; and they're scattered all over Britain and Ireland, from Kerry to Scotland's far north. Meet the P600s, and the man who bagged them all in 93 days._

* * *

**I first came across the P600s in 2018, while perusing hill-bagging.co.uk like any obsessive peak bagger. These peaks immediately captivated me for two reasons. Firstly, they encompassed all of the British Isles, rather than a specific country. Secondly, their sole criteria, a topographic prominence of 600m (1,968.5ft), distinguished them from most other mountain categories. When I found out there were only 10 known completers, but it was unclear what the fastest known time (FKT) was, I felt that this was a challenge to test myself against. I plotted an itinerary, complete with routes, based on the intention of ascending the 119 P600s as one continuous round.**

[![Image 6: Schiehallion summit selfie © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462568?fm=jpg&time=1757077529&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=eec428185bd0cd802c0f8acee887c023)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462568)

Schiehallion summit selfie

© Simon Tull

Since the original draft, the fundamentals of the challenge never changed:

*   I would follow direct out and back routes to each P600, so I would not complete many of their "classic" routes.
*   Sometimes the most direct route would entail ascending other categorised peaks along the way, but I would not go out of my way to do so.
*   I would ascend 2 P600s most days ("double peak days").

I created four distinct phases: starting with the 25 P600s in Ireland, my focus would then turn to the 16 P600s scattered across the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland. Afterwards, I would begin what I felt was the real challenge, the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland. The final stretch would take in the last 12 P600s spread across England, the Isle of Man and Wales.

> Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute

The itinerary itself was 92 days with almost every hiking day being a double peak day. The only exceptions were a triple peak day during Phase One, Ireland, and then single peak days for both Ben Alder and Snowdon, the latter being my final P600. I had designed the itinerary to be flexible as I was aware double peak days for most of Phase Three, the Scottish mainland, were not feasible as the routes during this stage were generally longer and with far more ascent required. Until I knew what I was capable of and what my daily limits for mileage and ascent should be, I would keep Phase Three as plotted, reasoning that it would be easier to spread out the P600s once the challenge was underway.

I was confident my schedules for Phases One, Two and Four were accurate, but given the above, my gut feeling was that Phase Three would take between 8-12 weeks, meaning the challenge could actually take up to 121 days.

![Image 7: P600s are scattered all over Britain and Ireland](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462569?fm=jpg&time=1757077584&dpr=1&w=553&sharp=7&s=ca92056b1d9e9d661fe3f89a3c677fe7)

I encountered a fellow enthusiast, Liam Chase, in mid-2019 whilst he was in the midst of his own bid to set the FKT for the P600s. I even joined him for a few routes. Liam was aware that we had the same goal, though our methods differed as he was completing his challenge on the weekends around his job. He would become the 15th person known to have scaled the P600s and, more importantly, the first to achieve this in a calendar year in 313 days.

My ambition persisted and every couple of years I would refine the itinerary when it felt like things were coming together to finally undertake this endeavour. After a couple of false starts, the stars began to align in late 2024.

Whilst I would ascend the P600s, Siobhan, my partner, would support me throughout the entirety of the challenge, most significantly by driving, as I cannot do this myself. I could have embarked on a self-powered feat by cycling between the P600s, but that would have at least doubled how long the challenge would last, if not more.

> I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham

The duration was also crucial for another reason: the challenge would be entirely self-funded. I had saved enough funds to cover our monthly commitments at home as well as our day-to-day spending during the challenge, based on the expectation that it could take up to 121 days to complete. Our continued employment was another consideration, as we envisioned this would be easier to secure if the challenge only took up to 121 days. After approaching our employers, I was granted a sabbatical but, sadly, Siobhan would have to leave her career of 10 years (an effective way to motivate me to finish it early!).

We originally intended to complete the challenge using a tent box mounted on our car. After testing this setup in early April, we thankfully had a reality check as to how optimistic we were being. Although ideal for short trips, the tent box was clearly not going to work for up to 17 weeks. We bought a converted van in mid-April, a fortnight before the challenge started. Alongside the van, we booked the occasional hotel whenever we needed some comfort, though in practice I was the one who needed this most.

[![Image 8: Combining sea cliffs and mountain tops on Croaghaun © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462571?fm=jpg&time=1757077957&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=17e5cd936383e64b6bb424ce2ea1030b)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462571)

Combining sea cliffs and mountain tops on Croaghaun

© Simon Tull

[![Image 9: Sgurr Alasdair's infamous screes © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462572?fm=jpg&time=1757077958&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=fbbbac1dee9eb6fef4b549abca01230d)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462572)

Sgurr Alasdair's infamous screes

© Simon Tull

In some respects, Phases One and Two would serve as a test bed, allowing us to adjust to and then fine tune what van life resembled to us, all the while figuring out how accurate our preconceptions about day-to-day life during the challenge actually were. In a similar vein, I had long considered Phases One and Two to be the final stage of my training ahead of what I strongly felt was the "real" challenge, Phase Three.

A couple of days before the challenge commenced, we sailed to Ireland. There was no going back. I just hoped that my middle-aged fitness and male grade navigation were enough to get me through!

> Despite hail and snow I smiled; there was nowhere else I'd rather be

#### Phase One – Ireland

_Friday 25th April to Thursday 8th May_

Journeying anti-clockwise around Ireland, I planned to ascend the 25 P600s located there in three blocks of four hiking days with a rest day wedged in between. It was wet and windy on Lugnaquilla, a fine start to the challenge and hopefully not a precedent. The weather was mixed for a few days until a four-week dry spell ensued that would last until late May. Barrclashcame would cement itself as the toughest ascent of the challenge, the measure against which future arduous ascents were compared. Croaghaun was the P600 that I was most looking forward to. Once I was near the summit of Ireland's highest sea cliff, the views I had longed to witness simply plummeted down into the ocean.

Phase One ended when we boarded the overnight ferry at Belfast, arriving in Liverpool the next morning. We had a 28-hour layover at home in Penrith before we needed to leave to catch another ferry. The short turnaround taught us a great deal about managing future returns, mainly that it was barely enough time to clean the van and our laundry!

[![Image 10: Bla Bheinn's summit trig © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462573?fm=jpg&time=1757078193&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=6cfa14dc18f852a996334809f7f88a1a)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462573)

Bla Bheinn's summit trig

© Simon Tull

[![Image 11: Snow-dusted Sgurr Mor (Fannaichs) © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462574?fm=jpg&time=1757078194&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=2b4f151971c84034502f39ccdb37cbe6)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462574)

Snow-dusted Sgurr Mor (Fannaichs)

© Simon Tull

#### Phase Two – Scotland (Islands and Peninsulas)

_Sunday 11th to Wednesday 21st May_

Phase Two was undoubtedly the most time-sensitive stage of the challenge, an 11-day odyssey of the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland, amidst which we needed to catch 16 ferries. The 16 P600s I would pursue were spread over two blocks of five hiking days with a single rest day in the middle.

We first hopped between Arran, Jura, Mull and the Ardgour peninsula. Despite years of refining my routes, Creach Bheinn was the first P600 where I identified a better route halfway through my own. Although this was bound to happen, I stuck to my route. The next day, I had my first setback. I was due to summit Garbh Bheinn and then Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill, but the former was a tough route. I moved Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill to the following day when I was due to be on the Knoydart peninsula, meaning Ladhar Bheinn would need to be rescheduled for later, an easy prospect as Phase Three would bring us near to Mallaig again. We finished up on Rùm, Skye, South Uist and Harris. Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute. It was slow progress heading up this immense scree gully, the hard work only becoming worthwhile by the amount of fun I had sailing back down in just 20 mins! I reached the 1/3 milestone on day 27 with Clisham, my 40th P600, before returning to the mainland.

[![Image 12: The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462576?fm=jpg&time=1757078448&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=143bb07ef4289bb99a873b8983eea891)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462576)

The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh

© Simon Tull

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)

_Friday 23rd May to Sunday 20th July_

Phase Three was split into a trio of subsections that were intended to make the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland more manageable. These subsections lasted 4.5 days, five weeks and 13 days respectively, with a break of three days at home in between each.

The first subsection was a loop around the far north of Scotland, just as the four-week dry spell came to an end. Things soon unravelled. After I descended from Canisp, I didn't feel strong enough to continue onto Ben More Assynt the same day, so I ended up ascending the latter the next day. When we returned to Penrith a few days later, I realised I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham and this had persisted ever since. In hindsight, rescheduling Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill during Phase Two was the first sign that I was tiring. Siobhan and I adjusted the portion sizes for all of my meals and this seemed to do the trick.

[![Image 13: Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462581?fm=jpg&time=1757078814&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=c4f3cba3313d2be14b69dc081dc1554e)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462581)

Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes

© Simon Tull

As mentioned earlier, a significant proportion of Phase Three should have been plotted as single peak days. Now that I knew my capabilities, I imposed daily limits of 18 miles and/or 7,500ft of ascent as I reworked the itinerary for the five-week subsection. Over half of my upcoming hiking days became single peak days.

Phase Three resumed as we proceeded to work down the Scottish mainland. I endured the harshest conditions that I have ever been exposed to during my back-to-back ascents of An Teallach: Bidein a' Ghlas Thuill and Sgùrr Mòr in the Fannichs. Despite having hail and snow driven into me by gale-force winds between 50-60mph, I responded as I would do every other time I was faced with hardship during the challenge, by smiling and laughing to myself, for there was nowhere else I'd rather be. After scaling Sgorr Ruadh, my 60th P600 and the halfway milestone on day 45, I surprised Siobhan when we checked into the Cluanie Inn as a halfway treat for a couple of nights around a rest day. By now, I had realised that I could feasibly complete the challenge in around 100 days by early August.

Suitably rested, we meandered into some remote glens west of Loch Ness before venturing to the far end of Loch Arkaig. This is when my second setback occurred. I was supposed to ascend both Sgùrr na Cìche and Càrn Mòr as part of a mammoth route as they stand on opposite ends of Glen Dessarry (these are the only two P600s which can be reasonably combined). I summited the former and wandered to the base of the steep grassy slope that started the long traverse to Càrn Mòr. Realising that completing my route would take longer than anticipated and having no way of updating Siobhan as I was out of signal, the correct course was to leave Càrn Mòr for another time.

[![Image 14: Sgùrr Eilde Mòr from Binnein Mòr © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462577?fm=jpg&time=1757078448&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=1a105f0717080ed55381645162c02624)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462577)

Sgùrr Eilde Mòr from Binnein Mòr

© Simon Tull

[![Image 15: The summit of Ben Lui © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462578?fm=jpg&time=1757078449&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=3faad703e514eaacf1ff0dcf3e94fa97)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462578)

The summit of Ben Lui

© Simon Tull

Whilst resting near Fort William, I reflected on the times when the isolation of hiking by myself on a tight schedule and in poor weather had begun to gnaw at me. I actually enjoy hiking in poor weather, so it was a telling sign as to how gruelling the conditions were. More so than any other point, I keenly felt the slow progress owing to the frequent single peak days, which, alongside the weather, made this stage of the challenge the least enjoyable. In spite of this, I never turned back. I have no profound answer as to how I managed to stay motivated. My overriding impulse was that the challenge was what I had always wanted, and it was not meant to be easy.

It was fitting that Ladhar Bheinn was the first P600 I scaled after skipping Càrn Mòr. The following week saw me work my way back towards Fort William. On Gulvain, I met Arran Evison, who had recently started his own challenge to be the youngest person to complete the Munros on a mountain bike. It was a timely encounter given my recent introspection and afterwards, I felt a renewed conviction about myself. We then headed to the Cairngorms, where my uncle joined me for Ben Macdui, the first time I had been accompanied on a hike during the challenge. On day 68, I reached my 80th P600, Beinn a' Ghlò: Càrn nan Gabhar, the 2/3 milestone.

The five-week subsection ended with Ben Alder, the most intimidating P600, given that a 26-mile route is required to reach the summit. Of course, I headed up in heavy rain! Crossing the Allt a'Bhealaich Bheithe was fraught as the river was heavily in spate. There were some rocks to hop over on my way out, but on my return, I simply waded through the waist-deep water. After five weeks away, I just wanted to get home.

[![Image 16: Descending from Beinn an Lochain © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462579?fm=jpg&time=1757078574&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=3334d8d2ed050587e0a500bac1597ea9)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462579)

Descending from Beinn an Lochain

© Simon Tull

Upon deciding that Saturday 26th July would be the final day of the challenge, I adjusted the rest of the itinerary. There were 34 P600s left, so it would be a push to ascend these in 19 days, but doing so would mean the challenge would have taken me 93 days, an achievement that originally I did not believe was possible.

The remaining 22 P600s in Phase Three were split between two blocks of six hiking days separated by a rest day. Càrn Mòr was one of the first P600s I ascended after returning to Scotland for the last time. A heatwave then settled in as I marched up Beinn a' Chreachain, during which I became the proud owner of around 30 swollen horsefly bites. Our final two days in Scotland each had a yellow weather warning forecast, one for heavy rain on Saturday and one for thunderstorms on Sunday. Neither materialised and despite the threat looming overhead, it was eerily calm as I stood atop Broad Law, my 82nd and final P600 in Scotland, exactly 10 weeks after summiting the first, Goat Fell.

In the following days, I had this feeling that the challenge actually ended on Broad Law. I can only put this down to two things. Up until the end of Phase Three, Siobhan and I had existed in an intense and tightly scheduled environment and although there were still 12 P600s left, Phase Four would be considerably more relaxed than what came before. Additionally, as I had strongly felt that the Scottish mainland was the real challenge for so long, in some ways, Phase Three had become "the" challenge.

[![Image 17: Longside Edge from Skiddaw at golden hour © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462580?fm=jpg&time=1757078574&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=cb72688ff540a6ab50bbb65ea97ff4c4)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462580)

Longside Edge from Skiddaw at golden hour

© Simon Tull

#### Phase Four – England, the Isle of Man and Wales

_Monday 21st to Saturday 26th July_

I was supposed to rest on the Monday before diving into Phase Four, the final stretch across the 12 P600s in England, the Isle of Man and Wales. Instead, I brought Skiddaw forward to make the Tuesday less crammed, meaning that I would finish the challenge on a 12-day stint as my last rest day had been on Monday 14th July.

I was joined on Scafell Pike and Cross Fell by Alex Staniforth, fresh from his own challenge in which he set a new FKT of 43 days for the Nuttalls. Having scaled the P600s in England, we then made fleeting visits to the Isle of Man and the Brecon Beacons. It was poignant that Wales was the last country we visited as this is where my love of hillwalking was first nurtured. The challenge concluded with a pair of triple peak days in Snowdonia, the first of which began with Aran Fawddwy, the only P600 which had the distinction of me failing to ascend it (twice!) before. After a brisk ascent of Glyder Fawr, we met my family at the Snowdon Mountain Railway station in Llanberis and waited for some others to arrive.

I was humbled by everyone who chose to be there for Snowdon, my final P600. We started up the Llanberis Path and met Siobhan and my family who had taken the train. Holding Siobhan's hand, I took a moment to reflect before touching the trig point that crowns Snowdon. Following a swift descent to Llanberis, I stopped my watch.

The challenge was over.

[![Image 18: Big team on Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa, the final P600 © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462575?fm=jpg&time=1757078194&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=0c866918434c9d021eec1221833e521f)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462575)

Big team on Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa, the final P600

© Simon Tull

#### Everyone loves fun facts, so here's a few about the challenge:

*   It took 93 days to complete (including 20 rest days)
*   I hiked 923.1 miles / the equivalent of 35.2 marathons
*   I ascended 359,154ft / the equivalent of 12.4 Mount Everests
*   I am the 16th person known to have ascended the P600s
*   I am only the second person known to have ascended the P600s in a single calendar year (the other is Liam Chase)
*   I am the first person to complete the P600s in the six years since Liam
*   I had only ascended 19 P600s before the challenge
*   Besides setting a new FKT, I smashed Liam's record by 220 days. We're still friends!

It was a privilege to raise funds for both Mind Over Mountains and Every Life Matters. I am grateful for their support in raising awareness of the challenge that I was taking on to support them.

I doubt that I will directly inspire the next person who vies to set a quicker FKT for the P600s, but I hope they ask me to be there on their last peak to shake their hand when they do. Records are meant to be broken, so I am excited for when I am surpassed.

As for what's next, setting a new FKT for the P600s was very much a once in a lifetime feat. I intend to reascend the P600s during my lifetime and complete their classic routes. Maybe I'll be the first person to complete a second round...?

# The P600 Challenge - Fastest round of the 600m-prominence peaks

![Image 3](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462576?fm=jpg&time=1757078448&w=576&h=275&dpr=1&sharp=10&crop=1079%2C515%2C0%2C386&s=2694448090f83853f1ff2edbfc12135b)

© Simon Tull

Share

[![Image 4](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462592?fm=jpg&time=1757089747&w=195&h=130&fit=crop&s=f5aaea5f5567b8a2f2377724df0c73d9)![Image 5](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462592?fm=jpg&time=1757089747&w=90&h=60&fit=crop&dpr=1&s=f05cc9c33e542d644c72d139ee03f1ee)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/user/profile.php?id=430538)[Simon Tull](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/user/profile.php?id=430538)

* * *

  
6th October, 2025

This has been read 4,214 times

* * *

Share

_Each rises 600m or more from its surroundings; there are 119 of them; and they're scattered all over Britain and Ireland, from Kerry to Scotland's far north. Meet the P600s, and the man who bagged them all in 93 days._

* * *

**I first came across the P600s in 2018, while perusing hill-bagging.co.uk like any obsessive peak bagger. These peaks immediately captivated me for two reasons. Firstly, they encompassed all of the British Isles, rather than a specific country. Secondly, their sole criteria, a topographic prominence of 600m (1,968.5ft), distinguished them from most other mountain categories. When I found out there were only 10 known completers, but it was unclear what the fastest known time (FKT) was, I felt that this was a challenge to test myself against. I plotted an itinerary, complete with routes, based on the intention of ascending the 119 P600s as one continuous round.**

[![Image 6: Schiehallion summit selfie © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462568?fm=jpg&time=1757077529&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=eec428185bd0cd802c0f8acee887c023)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462568)

Schiehallion summit selfie

© Simon Tull

Since the original draft, the fundamentals of the challenge never changed:

*   I would follow direct out and back routes to each P600, so I would not complete many of their "classic" routes.
*   Sometimes the most direct route would entail ascending other categorised peaks along the way, but I would not go out of my way to do so.
*   I would ascend 2 P600s most days ("double peak days").

I created four distinct phases: starting with the 25 P600s in Ireland, my focus would then turn to the 16 P600s scattered across the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland. Afterwards, I would begin what I felt was the real challenge, the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland. The final stretch would take in the last 12 P600s spread across England, the Isle of Man and Wales.

> Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute

The itinerary itself was 92 days with almost every hiking day being a double peak day. The only exceptions were a triple peak day during Phase One, Ireland, and then single peak days for both Ben Alder and Snowdon, the latter being my final P600. I had designed the itinerary to be flexible as I was aware double peak days for most of Phase Three, the Scottish mainland, were not feasible as the routes during this stage were generally longer and with far more ascent required. Until I knew what I was capable of and what my daily limits for mileage and ascent should be, I would keep Phase Three as plotted, reasoning that it would be easier to spread out the P600s once the challenge was underway.

I was confident my schedules for Phases One, Two and Four were accurate, but given the above, my gut feeling was that Phase Three would take between 8-12 weeks, meaning the challenge could actually take up to 121 days.

![Image 7: P600s are scattered all over Britain and Ireland](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462569?fm=jpg&time=1757077584&dpr=1&w=553&sharp=7&s=ca92056b1d9e9d661fe3f89a3c677fe7)

I encountered a fellow enthusiast, Liam Chase, in mid-2019 whilst he was in the midst of his own bid to set the FKT for the P600s. I even joined him for a few routes. Liam was aware that we had the same goal, though our methods differed as he was completing his challenge on the weekends around his job. He would become the 15th person known to have scaled the P600s and, more importantly, the first to achieve this in a calendar year in 313 days.

My ambition persisted and every couple of years I would refine the itinerary when it felt like things were coming together to finally undertake this endeavour. After a couple of false starts, the stars began to align in late 2024.

Whilst I would ascend the P600s, Siobhan, my partner, would support me throughout the entirety of the challenge, most significantly by driving, as I cannot do this myself. I could have embarked on a self-powered feat by cycling between the P600s, but that would have at least doubled how long the challenge would last, if not more.

> I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham

The duration was also crucial for another reason: the challenge would be entirely self-funded. I had saved enough funds to cover our monthly commitments at home as well as our day-to-day spending during the challenge, based on the expectation that it could take up to 121 days to complete. Our continued employment was another consideration, as we envisioned this would be easier to secure if the challenge only took up to 121 days. After approaching our employers, I was granted a sabbatical but, sadly, Siobhan would have to leave her career of 10 years (an effective way to motivate me to finish it early!).

We originally intended to complete the challenge using a tent box mounted on our car. After testing this setup in early April, we thankfully had a reality check as to how optimistic we were being. Although ideal for short trips, the tent box was clearly not going to work for up to 17 weeks. We bought a converted van in mid-April, a fortnight before the challenge started. Alongside the van, we booked the occasional hotel whenever we needed some comfort, though in practice I was the one who needed this most.

[![Image 8: Combining sea cliffs and mountain tops on Croaghaun © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462571?fm=jpg&time=1757077957&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=17e5cd936383e64b6bb424ce2ea1030b)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462571)

Combining sea cliffs and mountain tops on Croaghaun

© Simon Tull

[![Image 9: Sgurr Alasdair's infamous screes © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462572?fm=jpg&time=1757077958&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=fbbbac1dee9eb6fef4b549abca01230d)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462572)

Sgurr Alasdair's infamous screes

© Simon Tull

In some respects, Phases One and Two would serve as a test bed, allowing us to adjust to and then fine tune what van life resembled to us, all the while figuring out how accurate our preconceptions about day-to-day life during the challenge actually were. In a similar vein, I had long considered Phases One and Two to be the final stage of my training ahead of what I strongly felt was the "real" challenge, Phase Three.

A couple of days before the challenge commenced, we sailed to Ireland. There was no going back. I just hoped that my middle-aged fitness and male grade navigation were enough to get me through!

> Despite hail and snow I smiled; there was nowhere else I'd rather be

#### Phase One – Ireland

_Friday 25th April to Thursday 8th May_

Journeying anti-clockwise around Ireland, I planned to ascend the 25 P600s located there in three blocks of four hiking days with a rest day wedged in between. It was wet and windy on Lugnaquilla, a fine start to the challenge and hopefully not a precedent. The weather was mixed for a few days until a four-week dry spell ensued that would last until late May. Barrclashcame would cement itself as the toughest ascent of the challenge, the measure against which future arduous ascents were compared. Croaghaun was the P600 that I was most looking forward to. Once I was near the summit of Ireland's highest sea cliff, the views I had longed to witness simply plummeted down into the ocean.

Phase One ended when we boarded the overnight ferry at Belfast, arriving in Liverpool the next morning. We had a 28-hour layover at home in Penrith before we needed to leave to catch another ferry. The short turnaround taught us a great deal about managing future returns, mainly that it was barely enough time to clean the van and our laundry!

© Simon Tull

Snow-dusted Sgurr Mor (Fannaichs)

© Simon Tull

#### Phase Two – Scotland (Islands and Peninsulas)

_Sunday 11th to Wednesday 21st May_

Phase Two was undoubtedly the most time-sensitive stage of the challenge, an 11-day odyssey of the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland, amidst which we needed to catch 16 ferries. The 16 P600s I would pursue were spread over two blocks of five hiking days with a single rest day in the middle.

We first hopped between Arran, Jura, Mull and the Ardgour peninsula. Despite years of refining my routes, Creach Bheinn was the first P600 where I identified a better route halfway through my own. Although this was bound to happen, I stuck to my route. The next day, I had my first setback. I was due to summit Garbh Bheinn and then Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill, but the former was a tough route. I moved Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill to the following day when I was due to be on the Knoydart peninsula, meaning Ladhar Bheinn would need to be rescheduled for later, an easy prospect as Phase Three would bring us near to Mallaig again. We finished up on Rùm, Skye, South Uist and Harris. Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute. It was slow progress heading up this immense scree gully, the hard work only becoming worthwhile by the amount of fun I had sailing back down in just 20 mins! I reached the 1/3 milestone on day 27 with Clisham, my 40th P600, before returning to the mainland.

[![Image 12: The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462576?fm=jpg&time=1757078448&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=143bb07ef4289bb99a873b8983eea891)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462576)

The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh

© Simon Tull

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)

_Friday 23rd May to Sunday 20th July_

Phase Three was split into a trio of subsections that were intended to make the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland more manageable. These subsections lasted 4.5 days, five weeks and 13 days respectively, with a break of three days at home in between each.

The first subsection was a loop around the far north of Scotland, just as the four-week dry spell came to an end. Things soon unravelled. After I descended from Canisp, I didn't feel strong enough to continue onto Ben More Assynt the same day, so I ended up ascending the latter the next day. When we returned to Penrith a few days later, I realised I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham and this had persisted ever since. In hindsight, rescheduling Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill during Phase Two was the first sign that I was tiring. Siobhan and I adjusted the portion sizes for all of my meals and this seemed to do the trick.

[![Image 13: Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462581?fm=jpg&time=1757078814&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=c4f3cba3313d2be14b69dc081dc1554e)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462581)

Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes

© Simon Tull

As mentioned earlier, a significant proportion of Phase Three should have been plotted as single peak days. Now that I knew my capabilities, I imposed daily limits of 18 miles and/or 7,500ft of ascent as I reworked the itinerary for the five-week subsection. Over half of my upcoming hiking days became single peak days.

Phase Three resumed as we proceeded to work down the Scottish mainland. I endured the harshest conditions that I have ever been exposed to during my back-to-back ascents of An Teallach: Bidein a' Ghlas Thuill and Sgùrr Mòr in the Fannichs. Despite having hail and snow driven into me by gale-force winds between 50-60mph, I responded as I would do every other time I was faced with hardship during the challenge, by smiling and laughing to myself, for there was nowhere else I'd rather be. After scaling Sgorr Ruadh, my 60th P600 and the halfway milestone on day 45, I surprised Siobhan when we checked into the Cluanie Inn as a halfway treat for a couple of nights around a rest day. By now, I had realised that I could feasibly complete the challenge in around 100 days by early August.

Suitably rested, we meandered into some remote glens west of Loch Ness before venturing to the far end of Loch Arkaig. This is when my second setback occurred. I was supposed to ascend both Sgùrr na Cìche and Càrn Mòr as part of a mammoth route as they stand on opposite ends of Glen Dessarry (these are the only two P600s which can be reasonably combined). I summited the former and wandered to the base of the steep grassy slope that started the long traverse to Càrn Mòr. Realising that completing my route would take longer than anticipated and having no way of updating Siobhan as I was out of signal, the correct course was to leave Càrn Mòr for another time.

[![Image 14: Sgùrr Eilde Mòr from Binnein Mòr © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462577?fm=jpg&time=1757078448&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=1a105f0717080ed55381645162c02624)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462577)

Sgùrr Eilde Mòr from Binnein Mòr

© Simon Tull

[![Image 15: The summit of Ben Lui © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462578?fm=jpg&time=1757078449&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=3faad703e514eaacf1ff0dcf3e94fa97)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462578)

The summit of Ben Lui

© Simon Tull

Whilst resting near Fort William, I reflected on the times when the isolation of hiking by myself on a tight schedule and in poor weather had begun to gnaw at me. I actually enjoy hiking in poor weather, so it was a telling sign as to how gruelling the conditions were. More so than any other point, I keenly felt the slow progress owing to the frequent single peak days, which, alongside the weather, made this stage of the challenge the least enjoyable. In spite of this, I never turned back. I have no profound answer as to how I managed to stay motivated. My overriding impulse was that the challenge was what I had always wanted, and it was not meant to be easy.

It was fitting that Ladhar Bheinn was the first P600 I scaled after skipping Càrn Mòr. The following week saw me work my way back towards Fort William. On Gulvain, I met Arran Evison, who had recently started his own challenge to be the youngest person to complete the Munros on a mountain bike. It was a timely encounter given my recent introspection and afterwards, I felt a renewed conviction about myself. We then headed to the Cairngorms, where my uncle joined me for Ben Macdui, the first time I had been accompanied on a hike during the challenge. On day 68, I reached my 80th P600, Beinn a' Ghlò: Càrn nan Gabhar, the 2/3 milestone.

The five-week subsection ended with Ben Alder, the most intimidating P600, given that a 26-mile route is required to reach the summit. Of course, I headed up in heavy rain! Crossing the Allt a'Bhealaich Bheithe was fraught as the river was heavily in spate. There were some rocks to hop over on my way out, but on my return, I simply waded through the waist-deep water. After five weeks away, I just wanted to get home.

[![Image 16: Descending from Beinn an Lochain © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462579?fm=jpg&time=1757078574&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=3334d8d2ed050587e0a500bac1597ea9)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462579)

Descending from Beinn an Lochain

© Simon Tull

Upon deciding that Saturday 26th July would be the final day of the challenge, I adjusted the rest of the itinerary. There were 34 P600s left, so it would be a push to ascend these in 19 days, but doing so would mean the challenge would have taken me 93 days, an achievement that originally I did not believe was possible.

The remaining 22 P600s in Phase Three were split between two blocks of six hiking days separated by a rest day. Càrn Mòr was one of the first P600s I ascended after returning to Scotland for the last time. A heatwave then settled in as I marched up Beinn a' Chreachain, during which I became the proud owner of around 30 swollen horsefly bites. Our final two days in Scotland each had a yellow weather warning forecast, one for heavy rain on Saturday and one for thunderstorms on Sunday. Neither materialised and despite the threat looming overhead, it was eerily calm as I stood atop Broad Law, my 82nd and final P600 in Scotland, exactly 10 weeks after summiting the first, Goat Fell.

In the following days, I had this feeling that the challenge actually ended on Broad Law. I can only put this down to two things. Up until the end of Phase Three, Siobhan and I had existed in an intense and tightly scheduled environment and although there were still 12 P600s left, Phase Four would be considerably more relaxed than what came before. Additionally, as I had strongly felt that the Scottish mainland was the real challenge for so long, in some ways, Phase Three had become "the" challenge.

[![Image 17: Longside Edge from Skiddaw at golden hour © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462580?fm=jpg&time=1757078574&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=cb72688ff540a6ab50bbb65ea97ff4c4)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462580)

Longside Edge from Skiddaw at golden hour

© Simon Tull

#### Phase Four – England, the Isle of Man and Wales

_Monday 21st to Saturday 26th July_

I was supposed to rest on the Monday before diving into Phase Four, the final stretch across the 12 P600s in England, the Isle of Man and Wales. Instead, I brought Skiddaw forward to make the Tuesday less crammed, meaning that I would finish the challenge on a 12-day stint as my last rest day had been on Monday 14th July.

I was joined on Scafell Pike and Cross Fell by Alex Staniforth, fresh from his own challenge in which he set a new FKT of 43 days for the Nuttalls. Having scaled the P600s in England, we then made fleeting visits to the Isle of Man and the Brecon Beacons. It was poignant that Wales was the last country we visited as this is where my love of hillwalking was first nurtured. The challenge concluded with a pair of triple peak days in Snowdonia, the first of which began with Aran Fawddwy, the only P600 which had the distinction of me failing to ascend it (twice!) before. After a brisk ascent of Glyder Fawr, we met my family at the Snowdon Mountain Railway station in Llanberis and waited for some others to arrive.

I was humbled by everyone who chose to be there for Snowdon, my final P600. We started up the Llanberis Path and met Siobhan and my family who had taken the train. Holding Siobhan's hand, I took a moment to reflect before touching the trig point that crowns Snowdon. Following a swift descent to Llanberis, I stopped my watch.

The challenge was over.

[![Image 18: Big team on Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa, the final P600 © Simon Tull](https://img.ukclimbing.com/i/462575?fm=jpg&time=1757078194&dpr=1&w=617&sharp=7&s=0c866918434c9d021eec1221833e521f)](https://www.ukhillwalking.com/photos/dbpage.php?id=462575)

Big team on Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa, the final P600

© Simon Tull

#### Everyone loves fun facts, so here's a few about the challenge:

*   It took 93 days to complete (including 20 rest days)
*   I hiked 923.1 miles / the equivalent of 35.2 marathons
*   I ascended 359,154ft / the equivalent of 12.4 Mount Everests
*   I am the 16th person known to have ascended the P600s
*   I am only the second person known to have ascended the P600s in a single calendar year (the other is Liam Chase)
*   I am the first person to complete the P600s in the six years since Liam
*   I had only ascended 19 P600s before the challenge
*   Besides setting a new FKT, I smashed Liam's record by 220 days. We're still friends!

It was a privilege to raise funds for both Mind Over Mountains and Every Life Matters. I am grateful for their support in raising awareness of the challenge that I was taking on to support them.

I doubt that I will directly inspire the next person who vies to set a quicker FKT for the P600s, but I hope they ask me to be there on their last peak to shake their hand when they do. Records are meant to be broken, so I am excited for when I am surpassed.

As for what's next, setting a new FKT for the P600s was very much a once in a lifetime feat. I intend to reascend the P600s during my lifetime and complete their classic routes. Maybe I'll be the first person to complete a second round...?

## Summits on the Air Activation Report

**Activation Date:** Friday 26th September, 2025.  
**Activator(s):** Richard M1HAX.  
**Summit:** Butser Hill, Southern England, England.  
**Summit ID:** SOTA reference [G/SE-004](https://www.sotadata.org.uk/en/summit/G/SE-004) (1 point).  
**Summit Height:** 270m elevation, 158m prominence.  
**Summit Location:** Lat./Long. [50.97784, -0.98028](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=50.97784,+-0.98028). Maidenhead Grid `IO90mx`.  
**Distance:** 1.3km travelled with 35m of ascent.  
**Difficulty:** SAC Grade T1.([?](https://m1hax.uk/2019/01/swiss-alpine-club-hiking-grade-system/))  
**Elapsed Time:** 35m (including operating).  
**Weather:** 13°C, cloudy, 6kph NE wind, 75% humidity.  
**Radio Equipment:** Elecraft KX2, Elecraft AX1.  
**Callsign Used:**`M1HAX/P`.  
**Contacts:** 12 (20m SSB).

## Trip Notes

Butser Hill stands as the highest point on the South Downs chalk ridge at 270 metres, commanding views across Hampshire and beyond. The summit lies within Queen Elizabeth Country Park and holds considerable archaeological significance, with Bronze Age bell and bowl barrows, Iron Age cross dykes, and Romano-British field systems scattered across its slopes. The nearby Butser Ancient Farm has pioneered experimental archaeology since 1970, and virtually all modern reconstruction drawings of Iron Age settlements derive from research conducted there.

I tackled this summit en route to Portsmouth, where I would catch a ferry the following morning to activate the two SOTA summits on the Isle of Wight. The hill sits a short distance south of Petersfield, easily accessible from the A3 London Road dual carriageway. The barrier-operated pay and display car park (card payment only via ANPR) provides straightforward access to the summit.

Amateur radio operators should obtain written permission in advance from Hampshire County Council by emailing [qecp.enquiries@hants.gov.uk](mailto:qecp.enquiries@hants.gov.uk). The park rangers actively patrol and have approached previous SOTA activators operating without authorisation. Their concerns relate to verifying amateur radio licences and protecting the Scheduled Ancient Monument from ground disturbance - aerial guy pegs should not penetrate deeper than six inches.

From the car park, I walked north-east towards the antenna mast facility before following grassy trails to the true summit where the trig point stands. The car park was moderately busy but I encountered almost nobody during my walk across the hill. The cafe beside the car park was closed.

Setting up my Elecraft KX2 with the compact AX1 antenna, I found excellent activity on the 20-metre band. Despite the antenna’s compromised performance, conditions proved favourable and I worked twelve stations across Europe in quick succession. Highlights included regular chasers EA1DHB, EA2DT, and OH3GZ, along with Manuel HB9DQM - Swiss mountaineer and creator of the exceptionally useful [SOTLAS](https://sotl.as/) website.

The activation zone here is expansive with various operating positions available. Indeed, the blue badge parking bays reportedly fall within the activation zone, though SOTA rules prohibit operating from vehicles. On a clear day, the 360-degree panorama extends to the Isle of Wight, Spinnaker Tower, and the New Forest.

With nobody else in sight, I packed away my equipment and returned to the car within 35 minutes of arrival, continuing onwards to Portsmouth for the evening. This is a pleasant and easy hill, though the mandatory permission requirement and ranger patrols make it less suitable as a regular haunt for impromptu activations.
